interview.question: What is database sharding, and why use it?
interview.answer: Sharding distributes data across several databases, with each database holding a subset of the data. It can reduce per-database traffic and index size, and it can support parallel writes.
interview.followUp: What problem can occur with a geographic shard key? A region may grow faster than others, creating an overloaded shard. Rebalancing or a different shard key may be needed.

interview.question: How can data be divided among shards?
interview.answer: A shard key determines which database stores a record. Common examples in the documentation include a user’s last-name initial and geographic location.
interview.followUp: How can consistent hashing help? It can reduce the amount of data that must move when shards are added or removed.

interview.question: What are the main trade-offs of sharding?
interview.answer: Sharding makes application logic more complex. Cross-shard joins are harder, data can become unevenly distributed, and replication is still needed to reduce the risk of data loss.
interview.followUp: What happens if one shard fails? Other shards can remain operational, but records on the failed shard need replication or another recovery method to avoid data loss.

keyPoints: Each shard owns only a portion of the full dataset.
A system can add shards as the stored user data grows.
Splitting data can lower work on each database and improve cache behavior.
Smaller indexes can make lookups faster.
Separate shards can accept writes in parallel instead of using one central write point.
A failure in one shard does not necessarily stop all other shards.
gotchas: A shard can receive much more load than others when data is not distributed evenly.
Moving data between shards when the cluster changes requires extra coordination.
Queries that combine records from different shards are harder to design and run.
The application must choose the correct shard, which can make queries and routing more complex.

Single Point of Failure.summary: A load balancer distributes client requests across backend resources. Multiple balancers can improve availability, while routing rules can use health, load, cookies, or network and application data.
Single Point of Failure.explanation: A single load balancer can become a single point of failure. Using multiple load balancers in active-active or active-passive mode helps protect against that failure. The balancers distribute requests to healthy resources and can also terminate SSL or keep a client on one server.
Single Point of Failure.returns: The response from the selected computing resource, returned to the appropriate client.

useCases.title: Avoid failed resources
useCases.scenario: Some servers are unhealthy or overloaded and should not receive new requests.

useCases.title: Terminate SSL at the edge

useCases.title: Keep session affinity

interview.question: What does a load balancer do?
interview.answer: A load balancer distributes incoming client requests across resources such as application servers or databases. It returns the selected resource's response to the client and can avoid unhealthy or overloaded servers.
interview.followUp: What happens if the balancer fails? Use multiple balancers in active-active or active-passive mode so one failure does not stop traffic.

interview.question: How do Layer 4 and Layer 7 load balancing differ?
interview.answer: Layer 4 balancing uses transport information such as source and destination IP addresses and ports. Layer 7 balancing can inspect application headers, messages, and cookies before selecting a server.
interview.followUp: When might Layer 4 be preferable? It generally needs less time and computing power, while Layer 7 provides more routing flexibility.

interview.question: How does load balancing support horizontal scaling?
interview.answer: Horizontal scaling adds more servers instead of making one server larger. A load balancer sends requests across those servers, but shared data such as sessions may need a centralized database or persistent cache.
interview.followUp: How can sessions work without sticky routing? Store session data in a shared database or persistent cache so any server can serve the client.

keyPoints: A load balancer sends client requests to backend resources and sends their responses back to the correct clients.
Health-aware routing keeps traffic away from servers that cannot serve requests.
SSL termination moves encryption work from backend servers to the load balancer.
Routing can use methods such as random choice, least load, cookies, or round robin.
Layer 7 routing can use application-level information to choose a backend.
Adding servers lets the system handle more traffic, while the balancer spreads requests among them.
gotchas: A load balancer still needs enough capacity. Otherwise, it can limit the whole system.
Do not rely on only one load balancer when availability is required.
Scaling application servers can increase connection pressure on caches and databases.

SLA.summary: An SLA is not defined as a separate feature in this documentation. The page explains availability targets as uptime percentages, such as 99.9% and 99.99%, and shows their allowed downtime.
SLA.explanation: The page discusses availability as uptime or downtime expressed as a percentage. It describes targets with a count of nines, such as 99.9% or 99.99%, and gives the downtime allowed over several time periods. It does not define SLA terms, service credits, or an SLA declaration.

interview.question: How does the page quantify availability?
interview.answer: The page presents availability as the percentage of time a service is available. It describes 99.9% as three nines and 99.99% as four nines.
interview.followUp: What does 99.99% allow? The page lists about 52 minutes and 36 seconds of downtime per year.

interview.question: How do component relationships affect availability?
interview.answer: For components in sequence, total availability is the product of their availabilities. Two components at 99.9% each therefore provide about 99.8% overall availability.
interview.followUp: What changes with parallel components? The page gives the formula 1 - (1 - Foo) * (1 - Bar), which improves total availability.

interview.question: Compare active-passive and active-active failover.
interview.answer: Active-passive failover uses heartbeats and lets a standby server take over when the active server stops responding. Active-active failover lets both servers handle traffic.
interview.followUp: What is a trade-off of failover? It adds hardware and complexity, and replicated data may be lost if failure happens first.

keyPoints: Availability targets are often named by their number of nines.
A 99.99% target permits about 52 minutes and 36 seconds of downtime each year.
For sequential components, every component contributes another possible failure, so total availability goes down.
Parallel availability uses the chance that both components fail to calculate the remaining service availability.
Active-passive failover monitors the active server and uses a standby server for takeover.
Active-active failover keeps both servers serving requests instead of reserving one only for recovery.
gotchas: An SLA is not documented as a separate object or contract here. The page only explains availability measurement.
Adding failover or parallel components can increase complexity, so availability targets must include the whole service design.

Throughput.summary: Throughput is the amount of work completed in a unit of time. It is different from latency, which is the time needed for one action or result.
Throughput.explanation: Throughput measures how many actions or results a system completes in a unit of time. It differs from latency, which measures how long one action or result takes. A system should seek high throughput while keeping latency within an acceptable range.
Throughput.returns: The number of actions or results completed per unit of time.

interview.question: What is throughput, and how is it different from latency?
interview.answer: Throughput is the number of actions or results completed per unit of time. Latency is the time needed for one action or result.
interview.followUp: How can a system improve throughput? Add resources or parallel work, but check that latency remains acceptable.

interview.question: Can high throughput still produce a poor user experience?
interview.answer: A system can complete many operations over time while still making each user wait too long. Throughput describes total work over time; latency describes the delay for an individual operation.
interview.followUp: What metric would you inspect for a slow single request? Inspect latency, then find the part of the request path causing the delay.

interview.question: What performance goal does the guide recommend?
interview.answer: The target is not simply the highest possible throughput. The guide says to maximize throughput while keeping latency acceptable.
interview.followUp: Why should both metrics be measured? They describe different failure modes, so one metric cannot fully describe system performance.

keyPoints: Throughput counts completed actions or results during a time interval.
Latency measures the time required for one action or result.
A useful design goal combines high throughput with latency users can accept.
Heavy load can reveal a scalability problem even when one-user performance looks good.
gotchas: High throughput alone is not enough. Keep latency within an acceptable limit.

TTL.summary: TTL sets the maximum time a cached query result may stay in the cache before it is refreshed. It limits how long the result can remain stale.
TTL.explanation: TTL is the maximum time a cached result stays usable before the system refreshes it. In a query cache, the application can load a result, store it, and later replace it after the TTL expires.

interview.question: What does TTL mean in a cache?
interview.answer: TTL is the maximum time that a cached entry can remain before it is refreshed. It helps limit how long a query result can remain stale.
interview.followUp: What other cache update pattern could avoid waiting for expiry? Write-through updates the data store and cache together, so the cache does not become stale after a successful update.

interview.question: How does cache-aside work for query results?
interview.answer: A query cache can use cache-aside: check the cache first, load the result from the database on a miss, store it, and return it. Only requested data is added, which avoids filling the cache with unused data.
interview.followUp: What is the cost of a miss? It needs the cache lookup, a database read, and a cache write before returning the result.

interview.question: How can a query cache scale across machines?
interview.answer: A large cache can be split across machines by hashing the key to choose a machine. This uses memory more efficiently than keeping a full copy on every machine, but it adds complexity.
interview.followUp: What happens when a cache machine fails? Requests for its keys may miss, and a replacement node may add latency until its cache is populated.

keyPoints: Set a maximum lifetime for each cached result. This lifetime is the TTL.
With cache-aside, the application reads the cache first and fills it after a miss.
Sharding spreads cache entries across machines and is usually more memory-efficient than duplicating the full cache.

Vertical Scaling.summary: Vertical scaling increases capacity by choosing a larger server. Start simply, monitor resource use, and scale up when metrics show a bottleneck.
Vertical Scaling.explanation: Vertical scaling means moving a workload to a larger server instead of adding more servers. Monitor CPU, memory, disk input/output, and network use to find bottlenecks, then increase the instance size as needed.

example.code:

aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute \
  --instance-id i-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --instance-type "{\"Value\":\"m7i.large\"}"
example.explanation: This changes an EC2 instance to a larger size. Check resource metrics first, then choose a size that addresses the bottleneck.

useCases.title: Remove a bottleneck

interview.question: What is vertical scaling?
interview.answer: Vertical scaling increases the capacity of one server, such as by choosing a larger EC2 instance. It is simple and can be a good starting point for a small workload.
interview.followUp: What is the main alternative? Horizontal scaling adds more server instances, usually behind a load balancer, but it adds operational complexity.

interview.question: How do you decide when to scale vertically?
interview.answer: Use monitoring to identify the limiting resource before changing the server. Useful measurements include CPU, memory, input/output, and network usage.
interview.followUp: Why avoid scaling based only on CPU? Memory, storage, or network limits can be the actual bottleneck.

interview.question: What are the trade-offs of vertical scaling?
interview.answer: Vertical scaling keeps the design simple because the workload remains on one box. Its main drawbacks are high cost at larger sizes and the lack of redundancy or failover.
interview.followUp: When would horizontal scaling be preferred? It is preferred when higher availability or more capacity than one server can provide is required.

keyPoints: Increase capacity by selecting a larger server instance.
Use measurements to decide when the current server needs more capacity.
Check CPU, memory, input/output, and network metrics when looking for bottlenecks.
A single server is a reasonable starting design for a very small user base.
gotchas: A larger server can cost much more as resource needs grow.
One vertically scaled server does not provide a backup if it fails.
